rationale: The book's core claim — that 'the heart of the earth' in Matthew 12:40 denotes Jerusalem, the center of the land — is carried by the cited texts better than the strongest specific alternative (the tomb/Sheol reading). The decisive facts: (1) no Scripture ever calls a grave or the underworld 'the heart of the earth,' whereas Ezekiel 5:5 explicitly locates Jerusalem 'in the midst of the nations' and Ezekiel 38:12 uses tabbur ha'aretz ('navel of the land,' same word as Judges 9:37), so the book's referent has direct scriptural attestation and the tomb reading has none for the phrase itself; (2) the mirrored phrase inside the very typology Jesus invokes — Jonah's own 'heart of the seas' (bilvav yammim, Jonah 2:3) — is a locational idiom for the midst of the sea, and with the sea already defined as the nations (Rev 17:15), 'heart of the seas' = center of the gentile world mirrors 'heart of the earth/land' = center of the land, i.e., Jerusalem; (3) contemporary usage (Philo, Sibylline Oracles, Greek Ezekiel variants) confirms 'heart of the earth' was a known title of Jerusalem in Jesus' world; (4) the Jerusalem reading dissolves the notorious three-days-and-three-nights counting problem that the tomb reading itself created (Friday burial to Sunday yields only two nights), cohering with Luke 24:21's 'third day since these things were done.' The tomb/Sheol counter explains nothing that the Jerusalem reading cannot subsume — the tomb interval falls inside the Jerusalem interval, and the book independently accounts for the Sheol language (Jonah 2:2, Ps 16:10/Acts 2:27) through the swallowing-ruler symbolism (Jer 51:34,44) — while it requires the unsupported lexical step of equating 'heart' with grave/depth against biblical usage.
book_core_identification: 'The heart of the earth' (Matt 12:40) is Jerusalem — the city God set 'in the midst of the nations' (Ezek 5:5), the navel/center of the land (tabbur ha'aretz, Ezek 38:12) — so the 'three days and three nights' measure the Son of Man's time in the city from his arrest to his resurrection, mirroring Jonah's time in 'the heart of the seas' (the center of the gentile nations).
book_secondary_elaborations: The mirrored phrase argument: Jonah 2:3's Hebrew bilvav yammim ('heart of the seas') read via sea = peoples/nations (Rev 17:15) as the heart of the gentile world
The great fish as a devouring ruler/kingdom (Caesar/Rome), on the pattern of Nebuchadnezzar (Jer 51:34,44) and Pharaoh (Ezek 29:3; 32:2)
The scene-by-scene Jonah–Passion typology (sleeper in the storm, interrogation, innocent blood, lots, casting forth, gentile worship, mission to Nineveh, prophet's anger as Israel's envy)
The chronology claim that counting from arrest to resurrection satisfies 'three days and three nights' without calendar gymnastics (Luke 24:21), with the full calendar deferred to another work
Extrabiblical corroboration: Philo ('heart of the whole earth'), Sibylline Oracles ('navel and heart of the earth'), Greek Ezekiel variants
Day-as-thousand-years reading of Nineveh's 'three days' journey' (2 Pet 3:8)
Ninevites' rising as literal resurrection (anastēsontai) and the saints judging the world
strongest_counter_interpretation: The mainstream reading: 'the heart of the earth' means Jesus' burial in the tomb — and, in the fuller traditional form, his sojourn in Sheol/Hades — during the interval between death and resurrection. Its case: Matthew's explicit comparandum is Jonah 'in the belly of the whale,' and Jonah himself glosses that belly as 'the belly of Sheol' (Jonah 2:2), so the antitype should be the realm/state of death; Psalm 16:10 with Acts 2:27-31 applies Sheol/corruption language to Christ's burial interval; Eph 4:9 ('lower parts of the earth') and 1 Pet 3:18-19 supply the descent tradition; the 'heart of the sea' idiom can denote depths (Exod 15:8), permitting a subterranean sense for 'heart of the earth'; and the burial narratives (Matt 27:57-60) supply an obvious concrete referent.
counter_core_identification: 'The heart of the earth' = the grave/tomb, or more broadly the realm of the dead (Sheol/Hades), entered at Jesus' burial and left at his resurrection.
material_core_denial: The counter denies that the phrase refers to Jerusalem or the land's center at all: it holds that 'earth' means the ground/underworld rather than the land, that the interval runs from burial (not arrest) to resurrection, and that the referent is a place of death rather than the covenant city — the two identifications cannot both be the intended referent of the single phrase.
counter_case: Matthew 12:40 directly parallels the Son of Man's location with Jonah's confinement 'in the whale's belly,' a container of death-like confinement most naturally matched by the tomb
Jonah 2:2 — 'out of the belly of hell [Sheol] cried I' — Jonah's own prayer identifies the fish's belly with the death realm, grounding the Sheol/grave antitype
Psalm 16:10 / Acts 2:27-31 — apostolic preaching applies 'not leave my soul in hell... nor see corruption' precisely to the burial-to-resurrection interval
Ephesians 4:9 and 1 Peter 3:18-19 — the descent tradition reads Christ as going to the lower regions/spirits in prison after death
Exodus 15:8 — 'the depths were congealed in the heart of the sea' shows the 'heart of' idiom can denote depth, not only geographic center
Matthew 27:57-60; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4 — the burial supplies a concrete, narratively confirmed referent for the interval
book_explanatory_advantages: Scripture explicitly attests the book's referent: Ezek 5:5 ('This is Jerusalem: I have set it in the midst of the nations') and Ezek 38:12 (tabbur ha'aretz, navel of the land; cf. Judges 9:37) — whereas no biblical text ever calls a grave or Sheol 'the heart of the earth'

The mirrored phrase inside the cited typology: Jonah was cast 'into the deep, in the heart of the seas' (bilvav yammim, Jonah 2:3); with sea = nations (Rev 17:15), heart-of-seas/heart-of-earth form a matched pair — Jonah at the center of the gentile world, the Son of Man at the center of the land — making Jesus' phrase an exact echo of Jonah's own vocabulary rather than a novel idiom for burial

Contemporary usage confirms the title: Philo calls Jerusalem the 'heart of the whole earth,' the Sibylline Oracles 'the navel and heart of the earth,' and Greek Ezekiel copies substitute 'heart' for 'navel' — the phrase was a recognizable name for Jerusalem in Jesus' world

It dissolves the chronological contradiction the tomb reading created: Friday burial to Sunday morning cannot yield three nights, whereas arrest-night to resurrection can, cohering with Luke 24:21 ('the third day since these things were done' — plural events, not only burial)

It preserves and explains the fish symbolism separately and scripturally: the devouring ruler forced to give back what he swallowed (Jer 51:34,44; Ezek 29:3; 32:2; Acts 4:27; John 19:15), so the Sheol/death dimension is accounted for without collapsing 'heart of the earth' into the grave
It integrates the whole Jonah narrative that Luke 11:30 says constitutes the sign ('Jonah was a sign unto the Ninevites'), not merely the burial clause
counter_explanatory_advantages: Simplicity and tradition: the tomb is the obvious narrative referent of the death-to-resurrection interval and requires no symbolic apparatus
Jonah 2:2's 'belly of Sheol' gives the death-realm reading a footing inside the Jonah text itself
Continuity with the apostolic use of Ps 16:10 (Acts 2:27-31) and the creedal descent tradition (Eph 4:9; 1 Pet 3:18-19)
The 'heart of' idiom occasionally connotes depth (Exod 15:8), so a subterranean sense is not linguistically impossible
decisive_sources: Jonah 2:3 (Hebrew bilvav yammim, 'heart of the seas')
Luke 24:13, 21 ('the third day since these things were done')
Jeremiah 51:34, 44 (the swallowing ruler forced to give back)
Philo of Alexandria and the Sibylline Oracles (Jerusalem as heart/navel of the earth)
unresolved_objections: Matthew's explicit comparandum is Jonah 'in the whale's belly,' which Jonah 2:2 glosses as 'the belly of Sheol'; the death-realm reading retains genuine typological footing there, even though the book maps the fish to the devouring ruler rather than to the location
The 'heart of' idiom can denote depth (Exod 15:8 'heart of the sea' = the depths), so the subterranean sense of 'heart of the earth' is not linguistically excluded, only unattested for graves
The precise reconciliation of 'three days and three nights' counted from the arrest is asserted but deferred to an external work (Time Tested Tradition) not supplied in this bundle
Jesus was crucified and buried outside the city walls, so 'in Jerusalem' must be taken as the city with its environs / the land's center region rather than strictly intramural
Ancillary elaborations (day = 1000 years applied to Nineveh's three days' journey; Ninevites' rising as literal resurrection) are more speculative and are not needed for the core identification
